name: VTD-XML
workload: DOM parse wall-clock time on synthetic wide/shallow and deep/narrow XML files at 1KB-100MB, one Docker container per library, cross-language shootout of 14 XML libraries in 7 languages
claimed_speedup: 2.7x faster at 100MB (238.903ms vs 646.685ms), 4.9x faster at 10MB (21.45ms vs 104.783ms), 3.1x faster at 1MB (3.439ms vs 10.788ms) DOM parse time vs libxml2; loses at 1KB (0.036ms vs 0.013ms) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: VTD-XML: Java 21 (eclipse-temurin), Maven package build, no explicit JIT flags stated; libxml2: g++ via CMake Release build (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release), Debian bookworm
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner (exact CPU model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 35 stars on unofficial GitHub mirror jzhang2004/vtd-xml; canonical project is on SourceForge, latest release 2.12
tradeoffs: Requires a JVM; VTD's lazy/index-based model gives a fast DOM build but XPath queries afterward are then much slower than libxml2 (e.g. 3837.5ms vs 565.6ms at 100MB, derived from page data), so the win is DOM-parse-specific, not end-to-end; the project also ships native C/C++/C# ports per its site, but only the Java build was benchmarked here; dual GPLv2/commercial licensing, and the project homepage carries a notice terminating licenses for parties in litigation with XimpleWare.
caveats: Benchmark runs on shared GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runners with no stated CPU model, capping the tier at B; the win vs libxml2 is inconsistent by size (loses at 1KB), and vs pugixml specifically VTD-XML only wins at 100KB/1MB and loses at 10MB/100MB/1KB; canonical repo is on SourceForge so no verifiable last-commit date was found, hence maintenance_status is unknown.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/bemayer/xml-benchmark (orchestrator-flagged lead) -> bemayer.github.io/xml-benchmark/ rankings and per-fixture DOM Parse results

name: zxml
workload: DOM parse throughput (MiB/s) across 24 headline XML fixtures (real-world RSS/catalog/sitemap files plus the vendored pugixml test corpus and synthetic stress cases: deep trees, wide siblings, CDATA/attribute mixes), 5 samples x 40ms per fixture, 'stable' profile
claimed_speedup: 1.46x-9.73x faster DOM parse throughput than best-of {pugixml, rapidxml} per fixture (24/24 fixtures pass the >= max(pugixml,rapidxml) gate); e.g. pugixml_large.xml: 2560.26 MiB/s vs pugixml 473.25 MiB/s = 5.41x; average across fixtures 3799.40 MiB/s (ours-permissive) vs pugixml's 1312.83 MiB/s average = ~2.9x (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: zxml: Zig 0.16.0, ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native; pugixml/rapidxml (C++): system c++ driver, -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native
hardware: 12th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-12450H, Linux 7.2.2-zen1-1-zen, x86_64, CPU frequency scaling 47%, advertised MHz range 400.0-4400.0
tradeoffs: Zig-only API, no C ABI documented; default parser is destructive (mutates the input buffer in place) and permissive (may accept malformed XML such as an unescaped '>' inside a quoted attribute value); enabling validate_well_formedness roughly halves throughput (e.g. note.xml: ours-validated 1650.37 MiB/s vs ours-permissive 2802.99 MiB/s); no XPath support shown in README; extremely new and unproven with no external adoption yet.
caveats: This is the project's own benchmark suite (first-party), but it meets the Tier-A bar because compiler, flags, CPU model, and kernel are all explicitly stated and the benchmark code/results are public; the project itself cautions that 'a passing external gate does not establish the original absolute throughput objectives' (see its VALIDATION.md); 0 GitHub stars and a <2-week-old repo, so treat adoption/stability as unproven despite the rigorous, self-documented methodology.
found_via: WebSearch: 'fastest XML parser Zig OR "C#" benchmark faster than libxml2 2026' -> github.com/SmallThingz/zxml README Performance section and bench/README.md

name: quick-xml
workload: DOM Parse and SAX/Stream wall-clock time and throughput on synthetic XML files (1KB-100MB) plus DBLP/OpenStreetMap real-world extracts, cross-language shootout of 14 XML libraries in 7 languages, one Docker container per library on GitHub Actions
claimed_speedup: Beats libxml2 at every tested size on both DOM Parse and SAX/Stream, e.g. DOM Parse 100MB: 64.406ms vs libxml2 646.685ms (10.0x) and vs pugixml 112.874ms (1.75x); 10MB: 7.851ms vs libxml2 104.783ms (13.3x), vs pugixml 18.549ms (2.36x); SAX/Stream 100MB: 71.04ms vs libxml2 126.85ms (1.79x) (derived from page data); ranked #1 overall with aggregate score 93.0 vs pugixml 64.2 and libxml2 32.5
compiler_and_flags: quick-xml: Rust, release build implied by the benchmark harness (exact rustc flags not stated); libxml2/pugixml: g++ via CMake Release build (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release), Debian bookworm
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Already catalogued (KNOWN_LIST); this record only attaches a fresh, independent, monthly-refreshed cross-language Tier B benchmark showing it beating libxml2 and pugixml directly.
caveats: quick-xml is on KNOWN_LIST; reported only under the orchestrator's exception for new evidence on a known project (is_evidence_for_known=true). CPU model unstated (shared CI runner) and exact Rust build flags unstated, so capped at Tier B rather than A.

name: noyalib
workload: Criterion deserialize-to-Value-AST benchmarks on 5 fixtures (simple 3-field, nested 20-field, large_list 500 items, github_actions config, k8s multi-document) plus a SIMD structural-delimiter-scan microbenchmark on a 1MiB document
claimed_speedup: 1.11x-1.36x faster deserialize than yaml-rust2 across the 5 fixtures (e.g. k8s multi-doc 85.1us at 1.11x, simple 1.40us at 1.36x); also 1.42x-2.00x vs serde_yaml_ng/serde_yml/yaml-spanned/serde-saphyr; SIMD structural-bitmask scanner 4.2x (stable Rust) / 9.2x (nightly-simd) faster than a memchr delimiter-scan loop on a 1MiB document
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.95 stable (headline table) / rustc 1.98.0 (serde-saphyr head-to-head table); criterion --release, LTO=fat, codegen-units=1, panic=abort
hardware: Apple M4, aarch64-apple-darwin (headline table); Apple A18 Pro (serde-saphyr head-to-head table)
tradeoffs: Never benchmarked against libyaml or yaml-cpp (this task's named baselines) -- only against other pure-Rust YAML crates; the margin over its closest competitor (yaml-rust2) is modest (1.11x-1.36x) versus the larger headline figures shown against weaker competitors; zero-unsafe pure-Rust design trades some of that narrower yaml-rust2 gap for safety plus Spanned<T>/Cow<'a,str>/Value::Tagged features yaml-rust2 lacks; very new/low-adoption project.
caveats: baseline_in_list=false: yaml-rust2 is a widely-used pure-Rust YAML crate but not one of the five named incumbents (libyaml, yaml-cpp, toml++, libxml2, pugixml), and libyaml itself was never tested here. Numbers are entirely first-party (project's own criterion suite), though host/toolchain/flags are fully documented, meeting the Tier-A methodology bar on that basis. Results differ noticeably between the two disclosed hardware hosts (Apple M4 vs Apple A18 Pro), so treat exact ratios as approximate.
